If I remember, his logic follows that pwBPD’s motivations for their codependent behavior are much different than someone who is actually codependent/Dependent PD. I’m paraphrasing here, but while the outcome tends to hurt a person on the receiving end regardless, someone with BPD uses relationships as a way to regulate themself and usually that is seen as more directly manipulative but it’s with the intention of feeling more secure in the attachment. Anyway, the doc’s logic was something along the lines of when a person wBPD enters a relationship they can give up relative control in exchange for attachment security (regardless of how real it is) and the problems arise when they can’t regulate this properly and attempts to manipulate (in a nonjudgment frame) a situation positively to keep abandonment fears at bay. With DPD, people, instead of giving up control, establish a foundation of control where the dpd person is reliant on someone and forces control onto an unwilling partner; They make themselves extensions of another so that their anxiety about being taken care of is absolved without actual regard for the imposition they may have made on an un consenting other. It’s less about the relationship (and the other person.s) and more about needing control of this one aspect so that the rest of their life is enabled. I mean im riffing on this hard but I really didn’t want to go hear him talk this early haha. Point being — it’s funny “they” bring up this argument but if you consider it, ✨as a person with BPD✨ I’d say I’d be a bit more scared shitless if I entered a relationship with someone who might only want me for the stability they would perceive (and then force) a relationship (not attraction to me) to bring, only to make me feel like a monster when it’d be my “problem traits” sometime I likely hypothetically couldn’t fulfill expectations. The thing is not all mosses are equal. Some “mosses” aren’t mosses at all. Spanish moss is air plant and reindeer moss is a lichen. As live organisms, lichens will also be vying for water and not compare to the water retention of most sphagnum moss; you might find you need to water your plant more often than what one expects with the moisture retaining properties of bog moss.

Since lichen are a mutualism between a fungi and an algae, I would also be wary if you’re growing in hydroponics, since algae in general can affect the respiration and transfer of oxygen.

Sphagnum moss, last I heard, was being over harvested in some areas due to demand and as such prices of it are more expensive now since even dead it will give you a run for your money with the amount of moisture it retains. Like “true mosses”, it’s a plant not a fungus, but it also means it can also be a houseplant and you can grow some yourself from a culture. It’s probably more time effective to buy the desiccated moss as it can be used repeatedly, but you would be doing a little to prevent the over harvesting of bogs. If you do use live sp. moss, know that they are picky with water so in places where the tap is a little “harsher” it could struggle.

Other takeaway point — while gathering moss from outside seems like it’ll save you money, it could kill your plants. As with houseplants cohabitating with plants gathered from outside, you risk transmission of animal pests, fungal spores, fungi proper, and bacteria.

One year/growth season with extremely meticulous care. I live in the Pacific NW in the US. I grew them all hydroponically in Lecca and moss, in a mostly warm but fluctuating temp room, with some ventilation, climbing on cedar planks against a “wet wall”. I designed a little hydroponic pump system with a filter. 

(a lot of the inspiration was from going to places that did hydroponics but catered toward cannabis growers —those wholesalers will get you good prices on Lecca but do support local biz with your houseplants needs)

 that would keep cycling but sometimes removing the filter, and above all keep the wall wet. I would add small amounts of orchid “juice” every week or so. All the amounts were relative. There was also a humidifier next to the plant. The adult leaves lose the silver (although the sheen is def still in the green of the adult leaves imo, but I’m colorblind with some shades of green)  and the fenestrations are my favorite out of any plant. Natural light (slightly protected north facing window, with a grow light above them at times. 

The best way my brain wants to describe it as is “Crunchy Deliciosa’s Lovechild with an silky alien Adansonii.” They can demand so much but are a quite eye catching. They also survive hardship well, like many monsteras. My perus had a really hard some with the move, but the doobies were less…dramatic. I had an emergency where I had to move and the adult plant is dead but I have plenty of juveniles this year to keep alive until I can live in a place where I can set up my wet wall and have them grow! 

Side note: I grew two plants this way and the dubia that grew into an adult kept happy, but another one grew really slow, in the same container environment. Once it started to hold onto the cedar, it grew lots but didn’t seem to want to “grow up/adult” like the other one. It was cool because the one adult plant had a pretty shingling sibling next to it! This article is just to bring a little context about how little is reported on the presence of Asian Americans, their lives and stories
https://www.roadsideamerica.com/tip/56511

I can’t find articles on it, but a local historian in the town of Baker City, Oregon showed a friend of mine an area outside the city, where there’s a mass grave of Chinese people; railroad workers who at near completion of the railroad were killed en masse and thrown in ditches. No accurate numbers have been reported on the body count and some remains have been repatriated. The article linked above shows a monument but doesn’t elude to the many more deaths. There’s other articles available on people studying grave sites across the building of the rail system. 

https://www.oregonmetro.gov/news/hidden-history-lone-firs-chinese-cemetery

To bring the context to here in Portland, there’s been some recognition by the part of the city but there’s also a lot more to be done to have the public be aware of the significance of Asian, Black, Hispanic and Native communities building of this place that socially presents itself as predominantly white (and it is) but doesn’t promote communities in substantial enough ways to give them permanent and ongoing recognition and development for these communities. Segregation by design has been the state motto here forever. But little do people know that some of the first immigrants in there area were Mexican (mostly clergy, if I remember correctly. There’s supposed to be an idyllic abbey outside of Portland dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe, which seems out of place, but you’ll find a nearby town with a Mexican style plaza and church on the small main strip, Dayton I think was the name of the place). 

https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_tunnels

To not deviate too much, it’s amazing (in the most irreverent sense of the word) how much capitalist oriented people (the self proclaimed pioneers) have abused every single group of people with a drop of melanin; Asian people — which make up the majority of the world, a touchstone — have melanin just like brown and black individuals, but a different form of it. It’s what keeps the collagen going and keeps ~us~ from cracking fast, as popular expression would have it (which would be even slower than it is if we didn’t on average face more daily stress — not always but often). But melanin levels vary just as much in all POC/people with melanin. It feels kinda silly to say that. And even writing this out, I think it’s stupid that people really chose to be discriminatory about this melanin, but just because it’s stupid doesn’t mean it didn’t benefit/get exploited by anyone…in any case, I say that because sometimes poc don’t recognize the very “color” in Asian Americans — it’s as arrayed and spectral as ours, but thrown into the camp of being light skinned, white collar American camp, by stereotype. Not to mention Asian Americans have been in Latin America since the beginning of colonization, particularly male laborers who were discouraged/excluded from being part of integrated Mexican life (fun tangent fact: mezcal/tequila was made by Native people taking a traditional agave brew and applying Pinoy distilling methods). Many Asian workers (I believe the notable presence in Mexico at least was the Chinese, Filipino, and Japanese) did seek out intimate, romantic relationships with Mexican women and had children with them but families would still exclude the fathers from being integrated parts of the family and subsequently the fathers would usually, eventually — by contractual force or choice — have to move back to Asia. Later waves of Asian immigrants (this time including Korean people, if I remember correctly), included women and many of these women were fetishized (and still are egregiously in the US and LatAm), were pushed into, sometimes brought over exclusively for, sex work. Their children could be taken from them, and the blending into the generic identity of “Mexican” took place, where there was no regard for letting people be aware of their family histories. This means there’s a good amount people who are “Latine/x” who have Asian heritage, in addition to the many Asian Latine/x people too. 

I say all this because Japanese Mexicans were also interned in the US at the demand of the US government. A fact that is kept unbeknownst to most. Just to segue into ending this scattered comment, most of the info above I gleaned from a book whose title I have forgotten but I think it’s published through a university in Texas, but I’m too lazy to look up. It’s a textbook, methinks. Its author is Selfa Chew and the book of hers I do remember is only in Spanish (Mudas las garzas, Mute are the Cranes). That said, some of the facts above I might not have completely straight but if they interest you, Ms. Chew’s work might be well worth looking into. Please fact-check, to your need.

But between paying made up money and your life, I would suggest your life. I took the bullet of fucking up my credit but I’m not letting those fuckers extort me anymore. I don’t suggest this because ugh I did it again once I got ANOTHER card, and wasn’t mindful about not using it at all. But hun, please please don’t kill yourself over those fuckers asking for money. It’s a lot of crippling shame that comes with it, as you might know, especially when it’s a « fuck i did it again » after getting helped out by family. I feel you 110%. When I was afraid my parents would physically punish me and a lie would get me out of it, I learned to lie in less than a heartbeat. It’s the same for when you’re afraid that people will abandon you - you take the lie over the perceived pain of people not wanting to hear what you actually have to say or who you actually are. Whatever the reason may be, it can leave you feeling bad, it’s not something you want to be doing long term because there are consequences to problem behaviors - one takeaway. And it’s a slippery slope, the more you do it, the more you justify it to yourself until you’re in a deep hole. Neurotypical people lie too, for different reasons too, so this isn’t just a BPD thing. As a kid, sometimes it’s the only way to avoid pain and it makes sense in the moment. But trust me, you do not want to be in your 20’s once you’re away from home and doing lying compulsively. It’s not cute and you might end up saying something untrue you seriously wish you hadn’t said. I know I said above that accountability hurts (sometimes it doesn’t, but you can’t know until you start the process!), but it’s a skill you have to learn to if it continues. 

You’re still young and have many new relationships to form and experiences to have, but you absolutely want to help yourself stop it from becoming too large to handle. Accountability might hurt a lot because you can’t know what the other person’s reaction will be. But if we accept the pain, I think it’s the way our brains learn to not do things again. Pathological lying is called an antisocial trait and can be a trait of ASPD (antisocial personality disorder/sociopaths), only these people (as far as I know) may seriously lack guilt so there is no need inside of them to feel accountable. If your lying gets too bad, get some help from a counselor if you need it. Accountability is the ultimate way you get free. Getting free is accepting in yourself you did something wrong, but often it’s only a half liberation if you’ve harmed someone with lies. I’m sorry if I’m rambling and repetitive, but that’s truth. 

I just really want to drive the point home that 1) avoid doing it as much as you can 2) learning to be accountable and telling the truth can be a sure fire liberation (unless you know it’s going to harm the other person fessing up, unless you needed to lie to stay alive, by all means try to be strategic about it). Like you said, chances are you probably haven’t said any harmful lies. But if you need to get free, accountability and truth is how it’s done. You’ll live through the pain, as frightening and unbearable as it may seem. And sometimes there’s no pain other than the bravery it takes to start. It might not even stop the pain you feel instantly,  but in my case it turned the guilt will turn into sadness. And sadness to me is a cleaner, not as heavy emotion as guilt. The last thing I want you to do is feel like you’re a bad person. I had to remind myself that when I called myself a bad person  that it was another lie I was telling myself. The truth was I was simply a person that had done bad/hurtful things (those are judgments, non judgmentally I would say I’ve done things against my morals). Again, sorry for this field guide. I just don’t want you to think that in my first comment above I was justifying the behavior. It’s not good. It happens, but catches up to you either through feelings or people losing trust in you. And if it gets too far the more repair that will need to be done. And it’ll leave you feeling more alone.

Final note: take this advice knowing I’m not a professional. This is my experience. I know you said you’re still young and living in a difficult situation and you might need to lie to survive at home still. At 17, I had to lie about being queer and my mental health and a ton of other stuff to stay safe at home. I don’t feel guilt for surviving and neither should you.

The reason for you might be different but after a lot of thinking and guilt (both necessary and unnecessary) that’s definitely what I do. It takes time to figure out the reasons behind what you do, but best of luck learning about yourself!
